clue.text: Flier in school about work, applications going in

indicators.note: the school's name is wrapped about the next part, holding it inside
the applications are said to go in, so they sit inside the word for work

blocks.note: Harrow is a famous English public school
op, short for opus, a musical work
uses are applications of something

explanation.surface: A pupil flies around school doing homework while applications pour in.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: applications go into the work, and that pair sits inside the school just after its first letter. Harrow is a famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: The common small brown bird is a creature that flies, so it is a flier in crossword terms.

clue.text: Lover now put out?

blocks.note: first meaning: a former sweetheart
second meaning, cryptic: a fire from the past that has since been extinguished

explanation.walkthrough: Put out suggests annoyed, but the question mark flags a literal reading: a fire extinguished.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a former partner, someone once loved, pictured as a blaze that has since gone cold.

clue.text: Belt it and belt up!

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
belt up is British slang for be quiet, and sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: An exasperated order to fasten a seatbelt and stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' meaning sex appeal is an old crossword convention giving SA.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a broad band of cloth worn around the waist or across the body, a kind of belt.

clue.text: Unholy carcass, not divine

indicators.note: an unholy mess is a chaotic one, so the following letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dead body that is unholy and not divine at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unholy' and 'not divine' seem to say the same thing, but Unholy is the signal and divine is the definition, meaning the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sacrosanct is too sacred to be violated, treated as holy and beyond question.

clue.text: Fly through Thailand's capital in aeroplane after vacation

indicators.note: a capital is the head letter of a word, so only Thailand's first is used
vacated means emptied, so the word loses everything but its outside letters
these pieces are placed in the emptied word, which surrounds them

blocks.note: aeroplane with its middle cleared out
via means by way of, or through
the head letter of Thailand

explanation.surface: Flying via Bangkok in a plane after a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: VIA and T go inside A...E, the shell of aeroplane. 'Vacation' tempts as a holiday, but it means emptying.
explanation.definitionFit: To aviate is to pilot or travel in an aircraft, a formal verb for flying.

clue.text: Forest team, a football team

blocks.note: first meaning: a group of wardens who patrol woodland
second meaning: a club such as Glasgow ... or Queens Park ...

explanation.walkthrough: Forest suggests Nottingham Forest, an English football club, but here it is literal woodland. Rangers is a Glasgow football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Park and woodland wardens are called rangers, and several football clubs, notably in Glasgow, carry that name.

clue.text: Killed when upset, stray bitten by their rabid dog

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top
rabid means wild and frenzied, so the letters run amok into a new order
something bitten is held between the teeth, so one piece is gripped inside the other

blocks.note: slew is the past tense of slay, to kill
to err is to stray from the right path
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rabid dog has bitten a stray and killed it.
explanation.walkthrough: Upset suits a down clue, where the word is turned upside down. The stray goes inside the rearranged word after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a breed of dog from Wales, a wiry black-and-tan terrier.

clue.text: American figure inferior to a novelist from England

indicators.note: inferior means lower down, and in a down clue being lower puts these pieces underneath

blocks.note: taken as written
US is short for United States, so American
ten is a number, or figure

explanation.surface: An American personality ranks below a celebrated English writer.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'inferior to' literally means placed below in the grid, not lesser in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice and Emma, and was a celebrated English writer of fiction.

clue.text: British money in question in France and Germany

blocks.note: qui is French for who, a question word
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: Converting British money is in question when travelling through France and Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In question' looks like a phrase on its own, but 'in France' marks QUI as a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Quid is British slang for one pound sterling, a unit of currency.

clue.text: Elastic in a closet in bits

indicators.note: elastic means stretchy and pliable, so the letters can be pulled into another shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Perished elastic found in a cupboard has broken into pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' that looks like a joining word belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sectional furniture is made of separate parts that fit together, so it comes in pieces.

clue.text: I run a lot, turning left for gateway to Europe and beyond

indicators.note: turning things over changes their order, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
port is the nautical word for the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A runner boasts of training hard, turning left on the route abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Luton is a town north of London whose airport handles many budget flights to the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: An airport is a point of departure for foreign travel, and this one serves many European destinations.

clue.text: Limitless, as tale no-one heard?

blocks.note: first meaning: too great to be counted or measured, as in vast wealth
second meaning, cryptic: a story never narrated to anyone

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second meaning: a story nobody heard was never recounted.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means immeasurably great, and literally describes a story that was never recounted to anybody.

clue.text: Tiny fraction supporting leaders in Tottenham Hotspur after match

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters, so only the starts of these words are kept
after places the letters from the football club behind the piece for the match

blocks.note: to be for something is to support it
a tie is a match or fixture, as in a cup tie
the initials of the London football club

explanation.surface: A small group of fans supports Tottenham Hotspur's leaders after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: A cup tie is a British term for a knockout match; Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: One part in forty is a small portion of a whole, so it is a little fraction.

clue.text: Now going for opening door

indicators.note: a door opening lets something in, so the first piece goes inside the next

blocks.note: ingress is a way in, an entrance or door
pro means in favour of, for

explanation.surface: Leaving now, heading for the open door.
explanation.walkthrough: Ingress, a formal word for an entrance, is split after its first two letters to let the second piece in.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means currently under way, happening at this moment, which is ongoing.

clue.text: Abnormally, Norman late for show

indicators.note: abnormal means not in the usual state, so the letters are put out of their usual order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Norman is unusually late for a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental things are decorative, present to look good rather than to serve a purpose.

clue.text: Rum say in barrel, simply rolled over

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows
something rolled over is turned the other way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: found across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A barrel of rum, simply rolled across the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum, capitalised by its position, looks like the drink but is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is a Scottish island, an example of an island, as 'say' signals.

clue.text: Wealth has to help poor artist

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so the words before it are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
RA stands for Royal Academician, a crossword artist

explanation.surface: A rich person is obliged to help a struggling artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A plethora is an abundance or excess, a great quantity of something, like riches.

clue.text: On top of that, a band from London

blocks.note: taken as written
the London Symphony Orchestra, a band of musicians

explanation.surface: Besides that, there is a group that comes from London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests a pop group, but here it is an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in addition or besides, adding one more thing to what came before.

clue.text: Jam lover

blocks.note: first meaning: to cram or force into a tight space
second meaning: informal word for a boyfriend or girlfriend

explanation.walkthrough: Jam lover reads as someone fond of a fruit spread; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to press or cram tightly, and as a noun it is slang for a romantic partner.

clue.text: Early potential shown by reliable bloke, builder

indicators.note: potential means what could yet become something, so the word is turned into another form

blocks.note: a brick is an old-fashioned British term for a dependable, good-hearted person
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dependable chap showed early promise as a builder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early potential' reads as early promise, but Early is the word to rearrange and potential is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bricklayer is a tradesman who builds walls from bricks and mortar, a construction worker.

clue.text: Unknown drone buzzed around there

indicators.note: buzzing around is flitting chaotically, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown quantities
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mysterious drone buzzed around over there.
explanation.walkthrough: Y as an unknown quantity is a common crossword convention borrowed from algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder is an old or dialect word for over there, at some distance but in sight.

clue.text: Thus has nailed clue for religion

indicators.note: to nail is to pin something down and hold it, so one word captures the other

blocks.note: so means thus, in that way
a hint is a clue

explanation.surface: Thus the solver has cracked the clue to identify a faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue is the setter's own wink at the solver: here it simply means a hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinto is the indigenous faith of Japan, centred on the worship of kami spirits.

clue.text: Estimated time to get system clearer?

blocks.note: a rough figure is an estimated one
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: An estimated timescale for clearing a computer system.
explanation.walkthrough: The system is the digestive system, not a computer, and the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dietary fibre keeps the digestive tract moving, so it helps clear out the bowels.

clue.text: One has bagged century now

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it and hold it inside

blocks.note: an ace is a one in a pack of cards
a ton is a hundred, a century in cricket

explanation.surface: A batsman has just scored a hundred runs.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a hundred runs by one batsman is called a century, or a ton; an ace counts as one in cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means immediately, without delay, so right this minute.

clue.text: Listen to this piano sonata, so tender, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word contributes its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of four consecutive words

explanation.surface: Someone urges a friend to hear a gentle piano sonata.
explanation.definitionFit: This whispered sound is used to attract someone's attention quietly, often before passing on a secret.

clue.text: Dealer and son go to pot plants

indicators.note: to go to pot is to fall apart, so the letters collapse into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drug dealer and his son are ruined by cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' and 'plants' suggest potted plants or cannabis; go to pot is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Oleanders are evergreen flowering shrubs, poisonous but popular in gardens, so they are plants.

clue.text: Retired minister, old, done!

indicators.note: retiring is withdrawing backwards, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
Rev, short for Reverend, the title of a minister

explanation.surface: An elderly minister, now retired, declares his career finished.
explanation.walkthrough: O comes first and the reversed REV follows.
explanation.definitionFit: When something is finished or at an end, we say it is over: the match is over.

clue.text: Catcher set for a very long run?

definitions.text: Catcher set for a very long run?

blocks.note: surface reading: a device for catching rodents, primed and ready
setter's reading: the Agatha Christie play that has run in London's West End since 1952

explanation.walkthrough: The device set for a mouse is also the name of the world's longest-running stage play, by Agatha Christie.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodent-catching device is literally a catcher, and the play of that name has a record theatrical run.
